subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 16 periods = 640 minutes
Total: 16 periods · 10h 40min

repairs.why:
ARV-D-119, partial: the standard's last two teaching units are a PAIR — U15 'Cultural Fair — Research and Prepare' MAKES the posters, U16 (the mandated synthesis) presents them ('materials: Group posters and charts prepared previously'). The X-1+1 form at X=15 serves U1..U14 + the synthesis and drops U15, so the closer needs posters no unit in that plan ever made. Swapping U14 and U15 puts the poster-making inside the X=15 prefix. Founder ruling 2026-08-11, declared a ONE-OFF on the TOP canonical alone.
SAFE: the two units are mutually independent and both sit on the same section ('Spirit of Togetherness'), so no anchor, registry, first-visit order or contiguity fact moves. U14 (Local Contributors) sources elders and community and names no Cultural Fair content; U15 sources Textbook p. 92 and family knowledge and names no Local Contributors content; each already closes on its own ground. Rule 3's cap survives (…O&R · C&E · HI · D&C — no run of two).
SCOPE, STATED: this does NOT fix X=14, which serves the prefix of 13 and drops BOTH units whatever their order. X=14 needs the poster unit at position <=13 — a three-unit move, not this swap — and stays open on ARV-D-119.

repairs.reason: C3 defect repair (testing.md C3 · S4 mathematics·secondary). Generic passes derive their value from the summary, the Pedagogy document or the schema; declared edits are hand-written per instance and listed with their defect id. No pedagogical content was regenerated: register and continuity edits delete or rephrase a clause whose content is already named, and word-count edits shorten a label without adding a fact.

edits.new: Name one traditional headgear worn in a particular region of India. In two or three sentences, explain why that headgear suits the region it comes from, and what it tells us about the people who wear it.

periods.textbook_anchor: A Special Day in School — Students write about special events and activities that take place at their school on Republic Day (p. 76)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure of the National Flag (p. 76)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens by asking students to close their eyes and picture a Republic Day morning at school — the flagpole, the crowd, the anthem. A few students share memories aloud, and the teacher draws out what made the occasion feel different from an ordinary school day.

Students open Textbook p. 76 and read the opening scene together. The teacher pauses to ask: what does each colour on the flag mean to you before checking with the text? The class reads the significance of saffron, white (with the Ashoka Chakra), and green, and students jot the meanings in their notebooks.

Students respond individually in writing to the prompt on Textbook p. 76 — what special events or activities take place at their school on Republic Day. After writing, three or four volunteers share; the teacher notes recurring and unique events on the board, helping the class see that schools across India may celebrate differently yet share the same occasion.

Class discussion: why does the country need a Constitution, and why was 26 January 1950 chosen? The teacher connects 15 August 1947 (freedom) to the need for a governing set of rules, then closes by asking students to think of one rule their school has and why it matters — leaving that thought open for personal reflection.

periods.implied_lo: Students can describe a national celebration and connect its symbolic elements to shared civic values.
periods.section_context: Republic Day celebration at school, significance of flag colours — saffron, white, green — the Ashoka Chakra, and India's Constitution adopted on 26 January 1950.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone in your family ever stood at a flagpole on Republic Day somewhere other than school — a government office, a village square?' Drawing out these family memories surfaces the tradition as a living community practice rather than only a school event.

periods.activity_title: Rivers and Mountains in the Anthem
periods.textbook_anchor: A Special Day in School — Students name rivers and mountain ranges mentioned in the National Anthem and fill in the table (p. 77)
materials: Political map of India (classroom wall map or printed copy)
periods.visual_aids: Classroom wall map of India showing major rivers and mountain ranges

time_bands.activity: Teacher leads the class in singing or reciting the National Anthem together, then poses the question: do you notice any place names — rivers, mountains — hidden in the anthem's words? Students listen again (or read the transliteration on the board) and call out what they catch.

Students open Textbook p. 77 and work individually to fill in the table of rivers and mountain ranges mentioned in the anthem. The teacher circulates, prompting students to locate each feature on the classroom map — touching the map makes the geography tangible rather than abstract.

Pairs compare their completed tables, reconcile differences, and together try to add one river or range they know personally — from a home region, a family story, or a previous chapter's content. The teacher invites a few pairs to share their additions and trace them on the map.

Brief whole-class reflection: why would the writers of the National Anthem choose to name rivers and mountains? The teacher guides students toward the idea that natural features — rivers, plains, hills — are part of what makes India feel like one shared homeland, closing the unit on its own ground.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify and locate geographic features referenced in a cultural text and connect natural landmarks to a sense of shared national identity.
periods.section_context: Rivers and mountain ranges named in the National Anthem, filling the textbook observation table, locating features on an India map.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt: 'Does anyone's family come from near a river or mountain named in the anthem? Can you show us roughly where on the map?' This grounds the anthem's geography in students' own lived landscapes.

periods.activity_title: Our State Tableau — Poster or Model
periods.textbook_anchor: A Special Day in School — Students discuss and list items of their state tableau and make a poster or model of it (p. 78)

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: has anyone watched the Republic Day parade — live or on television? What part of the parade featured their own state? A short discussion surfaces what students already know about their state's tableau tradition, with the teacher noting key items on the board.

Students open Textbook p. 78 and use the discussion prompt to list the various items that appear in their state's tableau — costumes, crafts, monuments, animals, and cultural scenes. The class lists these together on the board, then each student or pair selects the elements they find most meaningful.

Students create a poster or a simple model of their state's tableau using available materials. The emphasis is on choosing symbols deliberately — students write or say one sentence about why each element they chose represents their state. The teacher circulates, encouraging students to draw on family or community knowledge of local crafts and celebrations.

A quick gallery walk around the room (or desks) lets students see each other's choices. The teacher closes by noting that together, all the state tableaux on parade day tell the story of one India — many parts, one celebration.

periods.implied_lo: Students can represent a cultural celebration through a creative artefact and explain the symbolic choices they made.
periods.section_context: State tableau items on Republic Day — costumes, crafts, monuments, cultural scenes — observed on television or in print and rendered as poster or model.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'What craft or art form is your state known for — something your family or neighbours might make or wear? Could that go into the tableau?' This draws out local craft traditions as living knowledge rather than textbook information.

periods.textbook_anchor: A Special Day in School — Students write five rules followed at school and propose one new rule (p. 79)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with the question: what would school feel like if there were no rules at all? Students respond freely, then the teacher steers the conversation toward why communities — from classrooms to countries — need agreed-upon rules. The link between a school's rules and a country's Constitution is introduced through the section's content.

Students open Textbook p. 79 and individually write down five rules followed at their school, then propose one new rule they would add and give a reason. The teacher encourages students to think about what the rule protects or enables — fairness, safety, cleanliness, inclusion.

Small groups of three or four share their lists and discuss: are any rules the same across all group members? Are any rules surprising to others? Groups identify the one rule from all their lists that they think is the most important, and prepare to explain why.

Each group shares their chosen rule and reasoning. The teacher draws the thread back: India's Constitution is the book of rules for the whole country — made by people, for people, to keep everyone safe and treated fairly. The unit closes on the idea that rules reflect what a community values.

periods.implied_lo: Students can identify the purpose of shared civic rules and connect the idea of school rules to the function of a constitutional framework.
periods.section_context: School rules as a parallel to India's Constitution, Independence Day and Republic Day as civic occasions, proposing a new rule and justifying it.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If a student proposes a rule about cleanliness or waste, gently connect it to what they know about Swachh Bharat Abhiyan — let the connection arise from students rather than being stated directly.

periods.textbook_anchor: Finding India in Currency Notes — Students observe a currency note carefully and fill in the observation table (p. 80)
materials: One Indian currency note per pair (any denomination)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook figure of currency note front and back (p. 80)

time_bands.activity: Teacher holds up a currency note and asks: what do you notice on this small piece of paper? Students call out anything they see — a face, a building, numbers, writing. The teacher lists responses on the board without confirming or correcting yet, building curiosity.

Students open Textbook p. 80 and, working in pairs with a real note, fill in the observation table — denomination, colour, languages printed, monument or building depicted, animals, and other symbols. The teacher circulates, prompting pairs to look at both sides and to notice features they might have overlooked, such as raised prints or the small spectacles symbol.

Class shares findings. The teacher draws attention to each symbol in turn: the portrait and watermark of Mahatma Gandhi, the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan spectacles (and its connection to Gandhi's cleanliness values), the National Emblem with three lions and the Ashoka Chakra, and the MANI app feature for visually impaired citizens. Students add or correct their tables.

Reflection: why would a country put its national symbols, historical figures, and civic values on everyday money that every citizen handles? The teacher closes on the idea that a currency note is a small museum of the nation's identity, carried in every pocket.

periods.implied_lo: Students can systematically observe an everyday object and record the civic, historical, and cultural information embedded in its design.
periods.section_context: Indian currency note — Mahatma Gandhi portrait and watermark, Swachh Bharat Abhiyan spectacles symbol, National Emblem with three lions and Ashoka Chakra, raised prints, MANI app, denomination, colours, languages, monuments, animals.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone in your family ever used the MANI app or noticed the raised prints? Who in our lives might rely on those features?' This opens a natural conversation about inclusion without making it a separate lesson.

periods.textbook_anchor: Finding India in Currency Notes — Students design an emblem for their school using symbols, words, shapes, and colours (p. 82)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook image of the National Emblem (p. 82)

time_bands.activity: Teacher revisits the National Emblem from the currency note — what message do the three lions, the Ashoka Chakra, and the motto send? Students identify the deliberate choices: animal for strength, wheel for dharma, motto for truth. The class then asks: what message would we want our school emblem to send?
Students open Textbook p. 82, read the design prompt, and take a brief moment to plan — what symbol, shape, colour, and words or motto they will use, and what each choice means.

Students work individually to design their school emblem, incorporating at least one symbol, one colour choice with a reason, and a short motto or words. The teacher circulates, asking students to articulate why they chose each element rather than simply complimenting the artwork.

A quick pair-share: each student shows their emblem and explains one symbolic choice to their partner. The teacher then holds up two or three contrasting designs and asks the class what different values or priorities each emblem seems to express — closing on the idea that symbols are deliberate, meaningful choices.

periods.implied_lo: Students can design a symbolic artefact and explain how each visual element communicates a chosen meaning.
periods.section_context: School emblem design using symbols, words, shapes, and colours — inspired by the National Emblem (three lions, Ashoka Chakra) and currency note design principles.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt: 'Is there a local tree, bird, or craft your school is known for in the neighbourhood? Could that be your symbol?' Inviting locally rooted choices makes the emblem genuinely meaningful rather than generic.

periods.textbook_anchor: Symbols that Speak — Students read riddles and guess the national symbols of India (p. 83)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook images of the tiger and peacock (p. 83)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the first riddle from Textbook p. 83 aloud without showing the page — students listen and call out their guesses. After revealing the answer, the teacher asks: why would India choose the tiger as its national animal? Students offer reasons; the teacher notes them without evaluating yet.

Students open Textbook p. 83 and work through both riddles individually, writing their guesses and one reason for each. The teacher then discusses the National Animal (tiger) and National Bird (peacock) — what qualities each represents and why these creatures feel like fitting symbols of India's natural heritage.

The teacher introduces the historical note about lions: once widespread across India, now surviving only in Gir forests of Gujarat. Discussion question: what does it mean that a national symbol animal is now found in only one place? Students connect this to what they know about conservation. The teacher closes the conservation thread without moralising — leaving the question open.

Students use the Find Out task on Textbook p. 83 as a starting point and brainstorm with a partner what they know about their own state's animal, bird, tree, and flower. The teacher notes that they will verify this with sources — this is an inquiry the class is opening, not closing today.

periods.implied_lo: Students can explain why particular animals or natural features are chosen as symbols and connect national symbols to conservation and cultural identity.
periods.section_context: National Animal (tiger), National Bird (peacock), National Emblem lion capital, Gir forests of Gujarat as the last lion habitat, riddles as a format for identifying national symbols.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does your state's animal or bird live near where you or your family come from? Have you ever seen it — in the wild, in a sanctuary, or in a picture?' Personal connections make the symbols vivid rather than abstract.

periods.textbook_anchor: Symbols that Speak — Students spot a tree, bird, animal, flower or object near their school, choose it as their school symbol, draw it, and write one line explaining why (p. 84)

time_bands.activity: Teacher takes the class on a brief, unhurried look around the classroom windows or the school veranda — students notice any trees, birds, or plants visible from where they stand. Back at their seats, each student names one natural feature they noticed and says one thing about it.

Students open Textbook p. 84 and read the Draw task. The teacher explains: the symbol should be something genuinely local — something a visitor to this school or neighbourhood would actually encounter — and the one-line caption should say why it deserves to represent the school.

Students draw their chosen natural element — tree, bird, animal, flower, or object — carefully and write their one-line caption below. The teacher circulates, asking each student about their choice: 'Why this one? What does it tell someone about our school or our place?' Students who finish early may colour their drawing.

A brief sharing round: five or six students hold up their drawing and read their caption aloud. The teacher notes the variety of choices on the board — if multiple students chose the same tree or bird, that itself becomes interesting: what does it tell us about our local environment?

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe their immediate natural environment, select a local feature as a symbol, and articulate in writing why it represents a community.
periods.section_context: Local tree, bird, animal, flower or object near the school chosen as a school symbol, drawn and captioned with a justification.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If students name a plant or bird that has a local folk name different from its common name, encourage them to write both — this honours local environmental knowledge carried in everyday language.

periods.textbook_anchor: Our Vibrant Culture — Students pick a word and find out what it is called in different languages spoken by classmates (p. 84)

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes the word 'mango' on the board and asks: who knows what mango is called in a language other than the one we use in class? Students call out words — the teacher writes each language name and its word for mango, building a multilingual list on the board before opening the textbook.

Students open Textbook p. 84 and read about India's more than a thousand languages and the Tamil word Māmpalam. The class then uses the Activity prompt to survey languages spoken by students in the room — each student writes their home language on a slip of paper or calls it out, and the teacher tallies them on the board.

In small groups, students extend the mango exercise to a second word of their choosing — they ask group members from different language backgrounds what that word is in their language, and record the results in a small table in their notebooks. Groups that include speakers of the same language look for differences in dialect.

Groups share one surprising or interesting discovery from their word survey. The teacher closes by connecting to the section's idea: each language carries its own songs, stories, and histories — India's linguistic diversity is not a problem to solve but a richness to celebrate.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a structured peer survey to document linguistic diversity and draw a conclusion about the relationship between language and cultural identity.
periods.section_context: Languages spoken by classmates, the word 'mango' in Tamil (Māmpalam) and other Indian languages, more than a thousand languages spoken across India, digital translation apps.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'In your family, do grandparents or elders use words from a different dialect or older form of a language that younger people don't use? Where did those words come from?' This surfaces the depth of language as living heritage.

periods.activity_title: Forest, Garden, and the Strength of Variety
periods.textbook_anchor: Diversity Everywhere — Students write about traditional Indian musical instruments they know (p. 89)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook images of percussion instruments — dhol, tabla, mridangam, dholak, thavil, idakka, khol, nagara, pakhawaj, dhama, khanjira (p. 89)

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws two quick sketches on the board — one with many different kinds of trees, one with only one kind. Ask: which do you think is more likely to survive a drought, a storm, or a pest attack? Students discuss freely; the teacher introduces the section's forest-versus-garden metaphor through student reasoning rather than telling.

Students open Textbook p. 89 and look at the images of percussion instruments — dhol, tabla, mridangam, dholak, thavil, idakka, khol, nagara, pakhawaj, dhama, khanjira. The teacher names each and, where possible, plays a short audio clip or imitates the rhythm. Students write down which ones they have heard or seen, and where.

Students write their response to the textbook prompt on p. 89 — what traditional Indian musical instruments they know — adding any instruments from their own region or family experience not shown in the textbook. Pairs then share lists and try to identify which region each instrument comes from.

Whole-class discussion: how does the range of instruments across India connect to the forest metaphor — each shaped by local materials, climate, and culture, yet all making music together? The teacher closes by asking students to hold this image of diversity-as-strength as they continue through the chapter.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect the metaphor of ecological diversity to cultural diversity and give examples of how regional variety enriches a shared national identity.
periods.section_context: Forest-versus-garden metaphor for diversity, percussion instruments — dhol, tabla, mridangam, dholak, thavil, idakka, khol, nagara, pakhawaj, dhama, khanjira — and their regional origins.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt: 'Has anyone in your family or neighbourhood played or made one of these instruments — or heard it at a wedding, a fair, or a festival? What was the occasion?' Lived musical memories make regional instrument diversity tangible.

periods.textbook_anchor: Diversity Everywhere — Students use a dupatta or scarf to help each other make a traditional headgear in small groups (p. 87)
materials: Waste materials — newspaper, paper bags, cardboard (for alternative headgear)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook images of saafa/pagri from Rajasthan and topi from Himachal Pradesh (p. 87)

time_bands.activity: Teacher shows the textbook images of regional headgear — the saafa/pagri from Rajasthan and the topi from Himachal Pradesh — and asks: what does the way people cover their heads tell us about where they live or who they are? Students make observations about colour, shape, and material before the teacher adds context about climate and tradition.

Groups of four or five are formed. Each group receives a dupatta or scarf and opens Textbook p. 87. The task is explained: try to fold or wrap the cloth to make a traditional headgear style — helping each other, not just one person working alone.

Groups work cooperatively to make their headgear. The teacher circulates, prompting students to discuss: where might this style come from, and why would that region's people wear it this way? Groups that finish the cloth version may also try making a second headgear from waste materials (newspaper, cardboard) as the alternative activity from the textbook.

Each group presents their headgear and says one thing about the region and tradition they were inspired by. The teacher briefly adds context on helmets and functional headgear — safety and occupation — connecting the idea that headgear always serves a purpose, whether cultural, climatic, or protective.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect regional clothing traditions to geography and cultural identity through a hands-on construction activity.
periods.section_context: Saafa/pagri from Rajasthan, topi from Himachal Pradesh, functional headgear including helmets, wrapping a dupatta or scarf in small groups, making headgear from waste materials.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask groups: 'Does anyone's family wear a particular kind of headgear for a wedding, a festival, or a specific occasion? What does wearing it mean in that context?' This draws out headgear as a marker of identity and respect, not just decoration.

periods.activity_title: Dance Forms on the Map of India
periods.textbook_anchor: Diversity Everywhere — Students identify and mark on the map of India the states where classical dance forms originated (p. 89)
materials: Outline map of India (one per student)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook map activity page (p. 89); classroom wall map of India

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: can you name any classical or folk dance of India — one you have seen, performed, or heard about? Students name dances; the teacher writes each on the board alongside the state it comes from, building a partial list before opening the textbook.

Students open Textbook p. 89 and read through the list of dance forms and their states of origin. Each student marks the states on their outline map, writing the dance form's name inside or beside the state. The teacher uses the classroom wall map to help students orient themselves — particularly for smaller states.

Students colour or shade the marked states using a simple colour key of their own choosing, then add a short legend at the bottom of the map. The teacher circulates, checking for accuracy and asking: 'Does this state share a border with the state whose dance form you marked just before it? What do you notice about where the dance forms cluster?'

Class discussion: are dance forms spread evenly across India, or do certain regions have multiple forms? The teacher draws attention to the diversity of classical and folk traditions as part of India's cultural landscape, and closes by noting that a map of culture is as rich as a map of geography.

periods.implied_lo: Students can read a list of cultural data and accurately represent it on a map of India, using symbols and a legend.
periods.section_context: Classical and folk dance forms of India, their states of origin, marking and labelling states on an outline map of India with a colour key and legend.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: If a student marks a state incorrectly, ask them to trace the state's border on the wall map first — spatial reasoning improves when students physically locate rather than just label.

periods.textbook_anchor: Spirit of Togetherness — Students identify which monuments appear on different currency notes and make a table (p. 91)
materials: Collection of Indian currency notes (various denominations, one set per group)
periods.visual_aids: Textbook images of currency notes and monuments (p. 91–92)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens Textbook pp. 91–92 and draws students' attention to the reflection prompts together — monuments on notes, the currency symbol, animals on the ₹10 note, and great Indians. The class makes a quick prediction table on the board before examining any actual note.

Groups receive a set of currency notes and open Textbook p. 91. They systematically record: which monument appears on each denomination, what the monument is and where it stands, the currency symbol of India, and the animals visible on the ₹10 note. Students fill a table in their notebooks, cross-checking with the textbook images.

Groups compare their tables with a neighbouring group. The teacher then leads a brief discussion on the great Indians shown on Textbook p. 92 — students identify who they recognise and share what they know about each person's contribution. The teacher fills gaps, keeping contributions concrete rather than hagiographic.

The teacher closes with a connecting question: why would a democratic country choose monuments and great people — rather than rulers or conquerors — for its currency? Students offer ideas; the teacher leaves the question as a thought to carry, not a conclusion to copy.

periods.implied_lo: Students can systematically record observations from a set of everyday objects into a structured table and use that data to draw conclusions about national values.
periods.section_context: Monuments on Indian currency notes across denominations, India's currency symbol (₹), animals on the ₹10 note, great men and women of India identified from textbook images.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Has anyone in your family or locality mentioned a freedom fighter or local hero who is not famous nationally? What did they do?' This bridges the national figures in the textbook to the local contributors students may know.

periods.textbook_anchor: Spirit of Togetherness — Class divides into groups, each assigned a different state, and prepares a presentation covering traditional dress, food, festivals, languages, dance or music for a Cultural Fair (p. 92)

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the Cultural Fair project from Textbook p. 92: each group will represent a different state of India and prepare a presentation covering traditional dress, popular food, festivals, languages, and dance or music. Groups are assigned states — the teacher ensures a spread across regions. Students discuss quickly within their group what they already know about their assigned state.

Groups begin research and preparation using textbook knowledge, their own family and community knowledge, and any available classroom resources. Each group creates a chart or poster covering the five areas: dress, food, festivals, languages, and dance or music. The teacher circulates, asking each group to identify one thing that makes their state unique AND one value or tradition it shares with other states.

Groups do a brief internal rehearsal — each member takes one area to present. The teacher notes which groups are ready and which need more preparation. The unit closes with the class understanding what the fair will look like — it is an inquiry that continues beyond this sitting, not something declared complete.

periods.implied_lo: Students can research cultural characteristics of a region collaboratively and present their findings through a creative group product.
periods.section_context: Cultural Fair project — group research on an assigned state covering traditional dress, food, festivals, languages, and dance or music — poster and oral presentation preparation.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt each group: 'Does anyone in our class actually come from your assigned state, or have family connections there? Their knowledge is the most valuable resource you have.' This values lived knowledge alongside textbook knowledge.

periods.textbook_anchor: Spirit of Togetherness — Students find out from elders about people who have contributed to the nation from their locality or state and share what they learnt in the classroom (p. 92)

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: when we think of great Indians, we usually hear the same few names. But every town, every locality, every family has someone who made things better for others — a teacher, a farmer, a healer, an activist. How would we find out who they were? Students brainstorm sources: elders at home, local library, community stories.

Students write in their notebooks: the name of one person from their locality or state who contributed to their community or the nation (this may be someone they recalled from home, a story they have heard, or an elder they spoke to before coming to school). For each, they write two or three sentences about the contribution.

Students share their entries in a round-robin format — each student names the person and one sentence about the contribution. The teacher notes names and contributions on the board, grouping them by type (education, environment, medicine, social justice, art). No contribution is ranked above another.

The teacher closes by returning to the chapter's thread — India's strength comes from people at every level, not only those whose faces appear on currency or in textbooks. The class reflects briefly on what it means to contribute to a nation, and the unit closes on its own ground.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a simple personal inquiry, record findings, and present them to peers as evidence in a structured discussion.
periods.section_context: Local and state contributors to the nation — identified through family elders and community knowledge — shared in classroom discussion and recorded in a board list.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Be prepared for students to name contributors from different communities, religions, and genders. Make the diversity of the board list visible: 'Look at how many different kinds of contribution are on our board — what does that tell us?'

periods.activity_title: Our Vibrant Country — The Cultural Fair and Chapter Synthesis
periods.textbook_anchor: Spirit of Togetherness — Groups set up a cultural fair in the class and discuss unique features and common values found across states (p. 92)
materials: Group posters and charts prepared previously
periods.visual_aids: Group-created posters and charts from all states represented

time_bands.activity: Groups set up their posters or displays around the classroom. The teacher explains the fair format: groups will present in turn, and after all presentations, the class will identify threads that run across all states — things India has in common beneath its differences.

Each group presents their state's cultural profile in turn — dress, food, festivals, languages, dance or music — to the class. Listeners note one unique feature and one shared value from each presentation. The teacher facilitates brief questions between presentations, keeping the exchange moving.

Whole-class synthesis discussion: the teacher collates the 'shared values' that students identified across states on the board. The class connects these threads to the chapter's core ideas — national symbols, the Constitution as shared rules, linguistic richness, ecological and cultural diversity as sources of strength, and India's heritage of yoga, ayurveda, and digital achievement alongside ancient traditions. The metaphor of threads woven into one fabric is invoked.

Each student writes one sentence: what 'Our Vibrant Country' means to them personally, drawing on anything from across the chapter. The teacher reads two or three aloud and closes: India's vibrancy is not despite its diversity — it is because of it.

periods.implied_lo: Students can synthesise observations from multiple regional examples to articulate the relationship between diversity and national unity.
periods.section_context: Cultural Fair presentations covering traditional dress, food, festivals, languages, dance or music of assigned states; shared values identified across states; unity in diversity as the chapter's organising idea.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: During the synthesis discussion, bring back specific content from across the chapter by name — the flag's colours, the currency note's symbols, the forest metaphor, the percussion instruments, the dance map — and ask students to trace how each connects to the idea of unity in diversity. Name the content, not any particular earlier activity.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can describe a national celebration and connect its symbolic elements to shared civic values.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Republic Day celebration at school, significance of flag colours — saffron, white, green — the Ashoka Chakra, and India's Constitution adopted on 26 January 1950.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: A Special Day in School — Students write about special events and activities that take place at their school on Republic Day (p. 76)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students share Republic Day school memories, read about the flag's colours and the Ashoka Chakra, write about their school's celebrations, and discuss why India's Constitution was adopted on 26 January 1950.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can identify and locate geographic features referenced in a cultural text and connect natural landmarks to a sense of shared national identity.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Rivers and mountain ranges named in the National Anthem, filling the textbook observation table, locating features on an India map.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: A Special Day in School — Students name rivers and mountain ranges mentioned in the National Anthem and fill in the table (p. 77)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students sing the National Anthem, identify rivers and mountain ranges mentioned in it, fill the textbook table, and locate each feature on a classroom map of India.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can represent a cultural celebration through a creative artefact and explain the symbolic choices they made.
coverage_handoff.section_context: State tableau items on Republic Day — costumes, crafts, monuments, cultural scenes — observed on television or in print and rendered as poster or model.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: A Special Day in School — Students discuss and list items of their state tableau and make a poster or model of it (p. 78)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students discuss their state's Republic Day tableau, list its symbolic elements, and create a poster or model — each student explains one symbolic choice.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can identify the purpose of shared civic rules and connect the idea of school rules to the function of a constitutional framework.
coverage_handoff.section_context: School rules as a parallel to India's Constitution, Independence Day and Republic Day as civic occasions, proposing a new rule and justifying it.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: A Special Day in School — Students write five rules followed at school and propose one new rule (p. 79)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students discuss why communities need rules, write five school rules and propose a new one, share in small groups, and connect school rules to India's Constitution.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can systematically observe an everyday object and record the civic, historical, and cultural information embedded in its design.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Indian currency note — Mahatma Gandhi portrait and watermark, Swachh Bharat Abhiyan spectacles symbol, National Emblem with three lions and Ashoka Chakra, raised prints, MANI app, denomination, colours, languages, monuments, animals.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Finding India in Currency Notes — Students observe a currency note carefully and fill in the observation table (p. 80)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Pairs observe a real currency note and fill the textbook observation table, then discuss each symbol — Gandhi's portrait, the spectacles, the National Emblem, raised prints, and the MANI app — and reflect on why a nation puts its values on money.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can design a symbolic artefact and explain how each visual element communicates a chosen meaning.
coverage_handoff.section_context: School emblem design using symbols, words, shapes, and colours — inspired by the National Emblem (three lions, Ashoka Chakra) and currency note design principles.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Finding India in Currency Notes — Students design an emblem for their school using symbols, words, shapes, and colours (p. 82)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students analyse the National Emblem's deliberate symbol choices, then design a school emblem with at least one symbol, a reasoned colour choice, and a motto — sharing and comparing with a partner.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can explain why particular animals or natural features are chosen as symbols and connect national symbols to conservation and cultural identity.
coverage_handoff.section_context: National Animal (tiger), National Bird (peacock), National Emblem lion capital, Gir forests of Gujarat as the last lion habitat, riddles as a format for identifying national symbols.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Symbols that Speak — Students read riddles and guess the national symbols of India (p. 83)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students solve textbook riddles to identify the tiger and peacock as national symbols, discuss why each was chosen, explore the conservation story of lions now found only in Gir, and begin inquiring about their own state's symbols.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can observe their immediate natural environment, select a local feature as a symbol, and articulate in writing why it represents a community.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Local tree, bird, animal, flower or object near the school chosen as a school symbol, drawn and captioned with a justification.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Symbols that Speak — Students spot a tree, bird, animal, flower or object near their school, choose it as their school symbol, draw it, and write one line explaining why (p. 84)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students observe their school's surroundings, select one local natural feature as their school symbol, draw it, and write a caption justifying their choice — sharing in a brief gallery round.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can conduct a structured peer survey to document linguistic diversity and draw a conclusion about the relationship between language and cultural identity.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Languages spoken by classmates, the word 'mango' in Tamil (Māmpalam) and other Indian languages, more than a thousand languages spoken across India, digital translation apps.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Our Vibrant Culture — Students pick a word and find out what it is called in different languages spoken by classmates (p. 84)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students survey languages spoken in the class, read about India's thousand-plus languages and the Tamil word Māmpalam, extend the survey to a second word of their choice, and discuss how linguistic diversity reflects cultural richness.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can connect the metaphor of ecological diversity to cultural diversity and give examples of how regional variety enriches a shared national identity.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Forest-versus-garden metaphor for diversity, percussion instruments — dhol, tabla, mridangam, dholak, thavil, idakka, khol, nagara, pakhawaj, dhama, khanjira — and their regional origins.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Diversity Everywhere — Students write about traditional Indian musical instruments they know (p. 89)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students work through the forest-garden metaphor for diversity, identify and record percussion instruments from Textbook p. 89, list instruments from their own regional experience, and connect instrument variety to the idea of cultural strength.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can connect regional clothing traditions to geography and cultural identity through a hands-on construction activity.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Saafa/pagri from Rajasthan, topi from Himachal Pradesh, functional headgear including helmets, wrapping a dupatta or scarf in small groups, making headgear from waste materials.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Diversity Everywhere — Students use a dupatta or scarf to help each other make a traditional headgear in small groups (p. 87)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Groups examine textbook images of regional headgear, cooperatively wrap a dupatta or scarf into a traditional style, discuss the regional and climatic reasons for the style, and present their creation with one cultural observation.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can read a list of cultural data and accurately represent it on a map of India, using symbols and a legend.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Classical and folk dance forms of India, their states of origin, marking and labelling states on an outline map of India with a colour key and legend.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Diversity Everywhere — Students identify and mark on the map of India the states where classical dance forms originated (p. 89)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students read the textbook list of dance forms and their states of origin, mark and label each state on an outline map of India, add a colour key and legend, and discuss the geographic distribution of classical and folk traditions.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can systematically record observations from a set of everyday objects into a structured table and use that data to draw conclusions about national values.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Monuments on Indian currency notes across denominations, India's currency symbol (₹), animals on the ₹10 note, great men and women of India identified from textbook images.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Spirit of Togetherness — Students identify which monuments appear on different currency notes and make a table (p. 91)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Groups examine currency notes of different denominations, fill a table of monuments, currency symbol, and animals, identify great Indians from textbook images, and discuss why a democracy chooses monuments and contributors rather than rulers for its currency.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can research cultural characteristics of a region collaboratively and present their findings through a creative group product.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Cultural Fair project — group research on an assigned state covering traditional dress, food, festivals, languages, and dance or music — poster and oral presentation preparation.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Spirit of Togetherness — Class divides into groups, each assigned a different state, and prepares a presentation covering traditional dress, food, festivals, languages, dance or music for a Cultural Fair (p. 92)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Groups are assigned an Indian state and prepare a Cultural Fair poster covering traditional dress, food, festivals, languages, and dance or music — rehearsing their presentation and identifying one unique state feature and one shared national value.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can conduct a simple personal inquiry, record findings, and present them to peers as evidence in a structured discussion.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Local and state contributors to the nation — identified through family elders and community knowledge — shared in classroom discussion and recorded in a board list.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Spirit of Togetherness — Students find out from elders about people who have contributed to the nation from their locality or state and share what they learnt in the classroom (p. 92)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students recall or record a local or state contributor identified through family or community knowledge, share in a round-robin format, and build a class board list grouped by type of contribution.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can synthesise observations from multiple regional examples to articulate the relationship between diversity and national unity.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Cultural Fair presentations covering traditional dress, food, festivals, languages, dance or music of assigned states; shared values identified across states; unity in diversity as the chapter's organising idea.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Spirit of Togetherness — Groups set up a cultural fair in the class and discuss unique features and common values found across states (p. 92)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Groups present their state's cultural profile at the Cultural Fair; the class identifies shared values across states and connects them to the chapter's key ideas — national symbols, the Constitution, linguistic richness, ecological and cultural diversity — closing with each student writing one personal sentence on what 'Our Vibrant Country' means.

assessment_items.question_text: The white stripe on India's National Flag has the Ashoka Chakra at its centre. What does the white stripe represent?

options.label: A
options.text: Dharma and justice for all citizens

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is C. The Ashoka Chakra appears on the white stripe but represents dharma — students who choose D have conflated the stripe's meaning with the Chakra's meaning, which is a common error from this section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can describe a national celebration and connect its symbolic elements to shared civic values.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing 'strength and courage' indicates the student has confused the meaning of the saffron stripe with the white stripe — a within-section mix-up of the three colours' meanings.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing 'growth and prosperity' indicates the student has confused the meaning of the green stripe with the white stripe — the same within-section colour-meaning confusion.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing 'dharma and justice' indicates the student has correctly associated the Ashoka Chakra with dharma but has transferred that meaning to the white stripe itself, conflating the stripe and the symbol it carries.

assessment_items.question_text: India's National Anthem mentions rivers and mountain ranges. Name one river and one mountain range mentioned in the anthem, and explain in one sentence why you think the writers of the anthem chose to include natural features.
expected_elements: One river mentioned in the National Anthem (e.g., Ganga, Yamuna, or another correctly identified river from the anthem text).
One mountain range mentioned in the National Anthem (e.g., the Himalayas/Vindhyas or equivalent correctly identified range).
A sentence connecting natural features to a sense of shared homeland or national identity — the idea that rivers and mountains are landmarks all citizens share.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any river or mountain range that genuinely appears in the anthem's lyrics; credit the student for correct identification even if spelling varies. The explanatory sentence is assessed for the idea — that natural features mark a shared homeland — not for exact wording. Regional variation note: students from different regions may relate more personally to different rivers or ranges; all are equally valid if present in the anthem.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify and locate geographic features referenced in a cultural text and connect natural landmarks to a sense of shared national identity.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

expected_elements: One river mentioned in the National Anthem (e.g., Ganga, Yamuna, or another correctly identified river from the anthem text).
One mountain range mentioned in the National Anthem (e.g., the Himalayas/Vindhyas or equivalent correctly identified range).
A sentence connecting natural features to a sense of shared homeland or national identity — the idea that rivers and mountains are landmarks all citizens share.

assessment_items.task: Think about your state's Republic Day tableau. Choose two elements that you would include in a poster of that tableau — for example, a costume, a craft, a monument, or a cultural scene. Draw or describe each element and write one sentence explaining what it represents about your state.
assessment_items.scaffold:
Element 1: [Draw or describe it here]
What it represents: _______________
Element 2: [Draw or describe it here]
What it represents: _______________
format_of_output: A drawing or written description of two tableau elements
assessment_items.annotation: Regional variation note: answers will vary by state and are all equally valid. Assess whether the student has chosen elements that genuinely represent regional identity (a craft, costume, or landmark associated with that state) and whether the explanatory sentence connects the element to the state's culture or history rather than stating only what the element looks like.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can represent a cultural celebration through a creative artefact and explain the symbolic choices they made.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can select culturally meaningful elements of a regional celebration and communicate their significance through a creative format — drawing on the section's connection between state identity and Republic Day tableau traditions.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The two-part scaffold prompts the student to make two deliberate choices and justify each. A strong response will choose elements that are specific to the state (a named craft, costume, or landmark) and provide a sentence that explains cultural or historical significance rather than only physical description.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: specific regional elements named (e.g., 'Kathakali dancer from Kerala because it is our classical dance form'), explanatory sentences that go beyond appearance to meaning. Weak: generic elements ('a flag', 'people dancing') without regional specificity, or explanatory sentences that only describe what the element looks like.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot draw may write a detailed description instead. Students who are unfamiliar with their state's specific tableau may describe a cultural element they know from their own family or community — this is equally valid as it demonstrates the same symbolic thinking.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Drawing or written description with written caption
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The Creative mode of this period asks students to make and explain symbolic choices — the same skill as analysing any designed artefact. Drawing or description are both valid outputs for this cognitive task.

assessment_items.question_text: A country's Constitution is sometimes called 'the book of rules for everyone'. Using what you know about India's Constitution and school rules, explain why having shared rules is important for a community — whether a school or a country. Give at least two reasons and one example from everyday school life.
look_for: At least two distinct reasons why shared rules matter — e.g., rules keep people safe, ensure fairness, resolve conflicts, protect everyone's rights, help a community function smoothly.
At least one concrete example from school life that illustrates one of the reasons given (e.g., a queuing rule, a cleanliness rule, a rule about taking turns).
A connection — even if implicit — between the school-level example and the idea that a country also needs a shared set of rules (the Constitution) for the same reasons.
A response that treats rules as something that benefits the community, not merely as restrictions imposed on individuals.
assessment_items.annotation: This item assesses civic reasoning, not recall of constitutional articles. A response that gives two sound reasons grounded in fairness, safety, or community function — even without using technical vocabulary — should be credited fully. Look for the student's ability to generalise from a familiar context (school) to a broader one (country).
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can identify the purpose of shared civic rules and connect the idea of school rules to the function of a constitutional framework.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

look_for: At least two distinct reasons why shared rules matter — e.g., rules keep people safe, ensure fairness, resolve conflicts, protect everyone's rights, help a community function smoothly.
At least one concrete example from school life that illustrates one of the reasons given (e.g., a queuing rule, a cleanliness rule, a rule about taking turns).
A connection — even if implicit — between the school-level example and the idea that a country also needs a shared set of rules (the Constitution) for the same reasons.
A response that treats rules as something that benefits the community, not merely as restrictions imposed on individuals.

assessment_items.question_text: Look at an Indian currency note carefully. Identify two different symbols or features on the note and explain what each one tells us about India.
expected_elements: Two distinct symbols or features correctly identified from an Indian currency note — e.g., Mahatma Gandhi's portrait, the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan spectacles symbol, the National Emblem (three lions), the Ashoka Chakra, raised prints, the MANI app reference, a monument, an animal, languages printed on the note.
For each symbol or feature, one sentence explaining what it tells us about India — its history, civic values, national identity, or commitment to inclusion.

At least one explanation that goes beyond naming the symbol to explaining its significance (e.g., not just 'Gandhi's face' but 'Gandhi's face reminds us of the freedom movement and the values he stood for').
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any two correctly identified features. Credit the student for the quality of the explanatory sentence — the item tests whether the student can read civic meaning into a designed object, not whether they can list features from memory. A student who correctly names a monument and explains which part of India it represents is demonstrating the same skill as one who discusses the Ashoka Chakra.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can systematically observe an everyday object and record the civic, historical, and cultural information embedded in its design.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

expected_elements: Two distinct symbols or features correctly identified from an Indian currency note — e.g., Mahatma Gandhi's portrait, the Swachh Bharat Abhiyan spectacles symbol, the National Emblem (three lions), the Ashoka Chakra, raised prints, the MANI app reference, a monument, an animal, languages printed on the note.
For each symbol or feature, one sentence explaining what it tells us about India — its history, civic values, national identity, or commitment to inclusion.
At least one explanation that goes beyond naming the symbol to explaining its significance.

assessment_items.task: Design an emblem for your school. Choose one symbol (an animal, plant, object, or shape), one colour, and a short motto (3–6 words). In the space below, draw your emblem and write one sentence for each choice explaining what it means.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My symbol: [Draw it here]
Why I chose it: _______________
My colour: _______________
Why I chose it: _______________
My motto: _______________
What it means: _______________
format_of_output: A drawing of the emblem including symbol, colour, and motto
Three explanatory sentences — one per element
assessment_items.annotation: Assess whether each choice is deliberate and explained — not whether the drawing is aesthetically accomplished. A student who chooses a local tree, a meaningful colour, and a motto that reflects the school's values, and who can articulate why, has fully met the implied outcome. Regional variation note: symbols, colours, and mottos will vary widely and all locally grounded choices are equally valid.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can design a symbolic artefact and explain how each visual element communicates a chosen meaning.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can make deliberate symbolic choices — selecting a visual element, a colour, and a motto that communicate a specific message — and articulate the reasoning behind each choice, mirroring the process of institutional emblem design introduced through the National Emblem and currency note.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The three-part scaffold (symbol, colour, motto) requires three separate explanatory sentences. A strong response explains each element's meaning, not just its appearance. Look for intentionality: the student should be able to say why this symbol, colour, and motto — not merely what they are.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: locally grounded or meaningful choices with explanations that reference identity, values, or aspiration (e.g., 'I chose blue for the sky because our school is always reaching upward'). Weak: arbitrary choices with no explanation, or explanations that only describe the element ('I chose a lion because it is strong') without connecting to the school's identity.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find drawing difficult may describe their emblem in writing in place of a drawing. Students who are uncertain about a motto may write it in any Indian language they are comfortable in — the thinking process is the same.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The creative-expressive mode of this period requires students to produce a designed artefact and explain it — both the product and the reasoning are part of the assessment.

assessment_items.question_text: Lions were once found across India. Today, wild lions in India survive only in one place. Where is that?
assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. All distractors are real and well-known Indian wildlife sanctuaries — Corbett (tiger), Sundarbans (tiger and mangroves), Kaziranga (one-horned rhinoceros) — so confusion is driven by genuine wildlife-sanctuary knowledge rather than guessing.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can explain why particular animals or natural features are chosen as symbols and connect national symbols to conservation and cultural identity.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing Corbett National Park indicates the student associated lions with tigers — Corbett is India's famous tiger reserve — revealing a confusion between the national animal (tiger) and lions.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing the Sundarbans indicates the student has recalled a prominent wildlife area from the same chapter or general knowledge but has not retained the specific detail about lions and Gir.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing Kaziranga indicates the student has recalled another famous Indian wildlife sanctuary (known for one-horned rhinos) but has not connected the conservation story of lions to Gujarat.

assessment_items.task: Look around your school — at the trees, birds, plants, or any natural feature you can see. Choose one as a symbol for your school. Draw it and write two sentences: one describing what it is, and one explaining why it is a good symbol for your school.
assessment_items.scaffold:
My chosen symbol: [Draw here]
What it is: _______________
Why it suits our school: _______________
format_of_output: A drawing of the chosen natural feature
assessment_items.annotation: Regional variation note: the natural feature chosen will vary by school location — a coastal school may choose a coconut palm, a hill-school a particular bird, an urban school a hardy tree in its compound. All are valid. Assess whether the justification sentence makes a genuine connection between the feature's qualities and the school's identity or values, not merely that it is nearby.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe their immediate natural environment, select a local feature as a symbol, and articulate in writing why it represents a community.

competency.competency_text: Presents observations and findings through different creative modes (drawing, diagram, poem, play, skit, oral and written expression)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student can move from direct observation of a local natural feature to a symbolic interpretation of it — explaining not only what it is but why it is meaningful as a community emblem. This mirrors the process by which national symbols were chosen.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The two-sentence structure separates description from justification. A strong response will have a justification sentence that goes beyond 'it is near our school' to say something about the feature's qualities (strength, beauty, resilience, seasonal presence) and how those qualities match the school's identity.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: a locally specific feature drawn with care, and a justification sentence that connects a quality of the feature to a value (e.g., 'The neem tree suits our school because it gives shade and healing, just as our school cares for us'). Weak: a generic drawing with no local specificity, or a justification that only states location ('It is in our school garden').
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who cannot draw may write a detailed written description of the feature. Students who are not sure which feature to choose may describe two and then explain which they would finally select and why — the reasoning process is what is assessed.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: Observation of the immediate environment followed by creative representation and written explanation is the core skill of this period — both the visual and verbal outputs are needed to demonstrate it fully.

assessment_items.question_text: In your class, students speak many different languages at home. How does this linguistic diversity make your class — and India — richer? Give two specific examples in your answer.
expected_elements: A clear statement that linguistic diversity adds richness — e.g., more words, stories, songs, and ways of seeing the world.

Two specific examples — these may come from the classroom language survey, the word-in-different-languages activity, or personal knowledge. Examples could include: learning the same word in multiple languages, hearing a song or story in a different language, understanding that each language carries its own history.
The response should treat diversity as a resource, not a challenge — it should not frame having many languages as confusing or problematic.
assessment_items.annotation: Regional variation note: the specific languages mentioned will vary by class composition and region — all are valid. Assess for the quality of the two examples (are they genuinely illustrative of richness?) and for the framing of diversity as a strength. A student who gives examples from their own classroom experience is demonstrating stronger engagement than one who gives only abstract statements.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a structured peer survey to document linguistic diversity and draw a conclusion about the relationship between language and cultural identity.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

expected_elements: A clear statement that linguistic diversity adds richness — more words, stories, songs, and ways of seeing the world.
Two specific examples — from the classroom language survey, the multi-language word activity, or personal knowledge — that illustrate how diversity enriches rather than fragments.
A framing of diversity as a resource rather than a challenge.

assessment_items.question_text: The section 'Diversity Everywhere' compares India's diversity to a forest rather than a garden. What is the main idea this comparison is trying to explain?

options.label: A
options.text: A diverse forest is stronger and more resilient than a garden with only one kind of plant, just as India's diversity makes it stronger.

options.label: B
options.text: A forest has more trees than a garden, so India has more people than other countries.

options.label: C
options.text: Gardens are artificial and forests are natural, so India prefers natural things.

options.label: D
options.text: India's forests should be protected just like its cultural traditions.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is B. This item tests whether students understood the metaphor's purpose — not its literal content. Distractor C is tempting because conservation is discussed in the same chapter, but it conflates two different ideas.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect the metaphor of ecological diversity to cultural diversity and give examples of how regional variety enriches a shared national identity.

competency.competency_text: Describes the relationship between the natural environment and cultural practices in their immediate environment (nature of work, food, festivals, traditions)

what_each_option_reveals.B: Choosing this option shows the student read the comparison literally (forest = more trees, India = more people) without grasping the metaphorical argument about resilience — a failure to read for meaning beyond surface content.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option shows the student connected 'forest' to the chapter's conservation content about tigers and lions, conflating a metaphor about cultural diversity with the separate theme of wildlife conservation.
what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option shows the student interpreted the forest-garden contrast as a value judgment about nature versus artificiality rather than understanding it as a metaphor for resilience through diversity.

assessment_items.question_text: Name one traditional headgear worn in a particular region of India. In two or three sentences, explain why that headgear suits the region it comes from, and what it tells us about the people who wear it.
expected_elements: The student names one type of traditional headgear from the section (saafa/pagri from Rajasthan, or topi from Himachal Pradesh, or another regional example).
The student identifies at least one reason why that headgear style is connected to the region — climate, cultural occasion, or material available locally.
The student makes a connection between the regional headgear tradition and the broader idea that clothing reflects where people live and who they are.
assessment_items.annotation: Regional variation note: students from Rajasthan or Himachal Pradesh may give more detailed personal knowledge of saafa/pagri or topi; students from other regions may name headgear from their own community. All are equally valid if they can explain the regional connection. Do not penalise for spelling variation in regional names.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect regional clothing traditions to geography and cultural identity through a hands-on construction activity.

competency.competency_text: Describes relationships (including between humans and animals/nature) and traditions (art forms, celebrations, festivals) in the family and community

expected_elements: The student names one type of traditional headgear from the section (saafa/pagri from Rajasthan, or topi from Himachal Pradesh, or another regional example).
The student identifies at least one reason why that headgear style is connected to the region — climate, cultural occasion, or material available locally.
The student makes a connection between the regional headgear tradition and the broader idea that clothing reflects where people live and who they are.

assessment_items.question_text: Your class marked the states of origin of classical and folk dance forms on a map of India. Look at where the dance forms are located. What do you notice about how they are spread across India? Write two observations.
expected_elements: Two distinct observations about the distribution of dance forms — e.g., dance forms are found across all regions of India (north, south, east, west, northeast); some states have more than one dance form; states in the northeast have distinct dance traditions; coastal and inland states have different styles.

At least one observation that goes beyond simply listing states — an inference about what the distribution tells us (e.g., 'every region has developed its own dance tradition', 'India's cultural diversity is spread across its geography').
Observations grounded in the map activity — not generic statements about dance being popular in India.
assessment_items.annotation: Assess for genuine map-based reasoning — the student should be drawing on the geographic spread they observed while marking the map, not simply recalling dance form names. Two well-reasoned observations grounded in spatial distribution earn full credit.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can read a list of cultural data and accurately represent it on a map of India, using symbols and a legend.

competency.competency_text: Reads simple maps of city, state, and country to identify natural and humanmade features (well, lake, post office, school, hospital) with reference to symbols and directions

expected_elements: Two distinct observations about the geographic distribution of dance forms across India — at least one that is spatial/map-based (not just a list of names).
At least one observation that draws an inference from the distribution — what it tells us about India's cultural geography.
Observations grounded in the map activity rather than generic statements about dance.

assessment_items.question_text: A student examining Indian currency notes of different denominations made a table of monuments shown on each note. What does including monuments on currency notes tell us about India?

options.label: A
options.text: Currency notes are the best way to teach people about architecture.

options.label: B
options.text: India uses its currency to share its heritage and national pride with every citizen who uses money.

options.label: C
options.text: India wants to show how many monuments it has compared to other countries.

options.label: D
options.text: The government chose monuments because they are easy to draw on small pieces of paper.

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is C. This item tests whether students understood the section's core idea — that currency note design is a deliberate civic act, not a decorative one. Distractor D is a plausible surface-level explanation that a student who did not engage with the section's meaning might choose.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can systematically record observations from a set of everyday objects into a structured table and use that data to draw conclusions about national values.

competency.competency_text: Observes and describes cultural diversity in their immediate environment (food, clothing, games, different seasons, festivals related to harvest and sowing)

what_each_option_reveals.C: Choosing this option shows the student interpreted the monuments as competitive display rather than as a communicative civic choice — missing the section's argument that currency is a vehicle for shared identity.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Choosing this option shows the student treated currency note design as primarily educational or instructional rather than as an expression of national values and heritage.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Choosing this option shows the student applied a practical/logistical explanation to a design choice that the section frames as deliberate and meaningful — a failure to read the design as intentional communication.

assessment_items.question_text: You found out about a person from your locality or state who contributed to the nation. Write the name of that person, describe one thing they did, and explain why their contribution matters — even if they are not famous nationally.
expected_elements: A name of a local or state-level contributor (may be a historical figure, a community leader, an artist, a freedom fighter, an educator, a health worker, or any person who contributed to society).
One specific description of what that person did — not just their profession but a concrete action or achievement.
An explanation of why the contribution matters — what it changed, helped, or protected for the community or country — even if the person is not widely known.
assessment_items.annotation: Regional variation note: answers will vary widely by region, community, and family background — all are valid. The item assesses whether the student can identify a contribution and articulate its significance, not whether the person named is verifiable from a standard list. Accept any person the student can describe with a genuine contribution, including family members or local figures not recorded in textbooks.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a simple personal inquiry, record findings, and present them to peers as evidence in a structured discussion.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: A name of a local or state-level contributor.
One specific description of what that person did — a concrete action or achievement, not just a job title.
An explanation of why the contribution matters for the community or country — what it changed, helped, or protected.

assessment_items.task: Imagine you are preparing a page for a Cultural Fair booklet about one state of India. Choose any state. Write about its traditional dress, one popular food, one festival, the language(s) spoken there, and one dance or music tradition. Then write one sentence about a value or tradition this state shares with the rest of India.
assessment_items.scaffold:
State: _______________
Traditional dress: _______________
One popular food: _______________
One festival: _______________
Language(s) spoken: _______________
Dance or music tradition: _______________
What this state shares with the rest of India: _______________
format_of_output: A completed profile covering all six fields
One connecting sentence about a shared value or tradition
assessment_items.annotation: Regional variation note: any Indian state may be chosen and all information is equally valid regardless of which state is selected. Assess whether the student has provided specific, plausible information for each category and whether the final connecting sentence makes a genuine observation about unity (not just 'all states are part of India'). Students who choose their own home state and draw on family knowledge should be credited for that depth of detail.
